units.name: The Living World: Ecosystems

concepts.intro: Energy enters ecosystems as sunlight and moves up trophic levels with large losses at each step.
b: Producers (autotrophs) capture energy by photosynthesis or chemosynthesis; consumers and decomposers get energy by eating other organisms or dead matter.
Only about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat through respiration and as waste.
Food webs show many feeding links; a food chain shows one path. Biomass and numbers usually shrink at higher levels (pyramids).
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is total energy captured; net primary productivity (NPP) equals GPP minus the producers' respiration.
Decomposers and detritivores recycle nutrients from dead material back into the ecosystem.

concepts.intro: Matter cycles through living and nonliving pools, and human activity speeds up or alters the flows.
b: Carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes CO2; respiration, decomposition and combustion return it; fossil fuels are a long-term carbon sink being released by burning.
Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification; fertilizers and fossil-fuel burning add reactive nitrogen.
Phosphorus cycle has no significant atmospheric phase; phosphate comes from weathering of rock and often limits growth in freshwater.
Water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration; groundwater can be stored for thousands of years.
Limiting nutrients (often nitrogen on land and phosphorus in lakes) control how much growth an ecosystem supports.

concepts.intro: Climate (temperature and precipitation) largely determines the distribution of biomes.
b: Tundra: cold, treeless, permafrost; boreal forest (taiga): cold, conifers; temperate deciduous forest: four seasons, rich soil; grassland: fertile soil, periodic fire.
Desert: less than about 25 cm of rain; tropical rainforest: high rain and biodiversity but nutrient-poor soil because nutrients are held in biomass; chaparral: dry summers, fire adapted.
Freshwater: lakes (littoral, limnetic, profundal, benthic zones), rivers, wetlands that filter water and buffer floods.
Marine: estuaries (mixing of fresh and salt water, high productivity), mangroves, coral reefs (sensitive to temperature and acidity), open ocean (large area, low productivity per area).
Lake turnover in spring and fall mixes oxygen and nutrients; thermal stratification forms in summer.

concepts.intro: These two processes link energy flow and carbon cycling.
b: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide plus water plus light energy produces glucose and oxygen.
Aerobic cellular respiration: glucose plus oxygen produces carbon dioxide, water and usable energy (ATP); anaerobic respiration and fermentation release less energy.
Producers do both processes; consumers and decomposers do respiration only.
These reactions keep atmospheric CO2 and O2 roughly balanced until fossil-fuel burning changes the balance.

traps: Energy flows in one direction and is lost as heat; matter cycles. Do not say energy 'cycles' through ecosystems.
Decomposers are not a trophic level that 'eats' the others for energy; they recycle nutrients from all levels.

units.name: The Living World: Biodiversity

concepts.l: Levels of biodiversity and ecosystem services
concepts.intro: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, and healthy ecosystems provide services to people.
b: Genetic diversity helps populations adapt to disease and change; species diversity includes richness (how many) and evenness (how balanced); ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats.

Ecosystem services: provisioning (food, timber, water), regulating (flood control, climate, pollination, water filtration), supporting (nutrient cycling, soil formation) and cultural (recreation, spiritual value).
Higher biodiversity generally makes an ecosystem more resilient to disturbance.

concepts.intro: Species number depends on island size and distance, and some species have outsized roles.
b: Larger islands and islands closer to the mainland support more species; small, distant islands have fewer.
Keystone species have an effect on the community far larger than their abundance (sea otters, wolves, beavers); removing them can restructure the ecosystem.
Indicator species signal ecosystem health; umbrella species protect many other species when their habitat is protected.
Specialists have narrow niches and are vulnerable to change; generalists adapt to many conditions.

concepts.intro: Human activities are driving species loss at rates far above background extinction.
b: HIPPCO: habitat destruction, invasive species, pollution, human population growth, climate change, overexploitation.
Habitat fragmentation isolates populations and creates edge effects; corridors can reconnect habitat.
Invasive species often lack natural predators and can outcompete native species (zebra mussels, kudzu).
The Endangered Species Act, CITES and protected areas are major conservation tools.

concepts.intro: Communities change over time after disturbance, and species adapt through natural selection.
b: Primary succession starts on bare rock or new land with no soil; pioneer species such as lichens build soil.
Secondary succession follows a disturbance, such as fire or farming, where soil remains, and proceeds faster.
Early successional species are fast-growing r-selected plants; later stages shift toward slower-growing, shade-tolerant species.
Natural selection acts on heritable variation; adaptations suit organisms to their environment.

traps: Keystone species are defined by their effect, not their size or numbers.
Primary succession needs soil formation; secondary succession starts with soil already present.

units.name: Populations

concepts.intro: Populations grow exponentially until limits slow them.
b: Exponential growth produces a J-shaped curve; logistic growth levels off at carrying capacity (K), producing an S-shaped curve.
Density-dependent factors (disease, competition, predation) intensify as density rises; density-independent factors (storms, fires) act regardless of density.
r-selected species have many offspring and little parental care; K-selected species have few offspring with extensive care and are more vulnerable to extinction.
Survivorship curves: Type I (most live long, die old), Type II (constant death rate), Type III (most die young).

concepts.intro: Demographers use rates and age structure to understand and project human populations.
b: Total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children per woman; replacement level is about 2.1 in developed countries.
Age-structure diagrams: a wide base means rapid growth, a straight-sided shape means slow or stable growth, a narrow base means decline.
Rule of 70: doubling time in years is about 70 divided by the percent growth rate.
Demographic transition: high birth and death rates, then falling death rates (rapid growth), then falling birth rates, then low and stable.
Growth rate = (birth rate - death rate) plus net migration, expressed as a percent.

concepts.intro: Resource use per person, as well as population, determines human impact.
b: IPAT: impact equals population times affluence times technology; wealthy countries have a much larger footprint per person.
Ecological footprint measures the land and water needed to supply a person's resources and absorb their waste.
Education and economic opportunity for women, access to family planning and lower infant mortality reduce fertility rates.

traps: Replacement-level fertility is above 2.0 because some children die before reproducing.
Do not confuse growth rate (a percent) with doubling time (years); use 70 divided by the rate.

units.name: Earth Systems and Resources

concepts.intro: Geologic processes shape landscapes and soil forms over long periods.
b: Divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries explain earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building.
Soil horizons from the top: O (organic), A (topsoil), E (eluviation), B (subsoil), C (parent material), then bedrock.
Soil texture depends on sand, silt and clay; loam balances them. Sandy soil drains fast; clay holds water but drains slowly.
Soil fertility depends on organic matter, nutrients, pH and the ability to hold water and nutrients.

concepts.intro: Uneven solar heating and Earth's rotation drive weather and climate.
b: Layers: troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone layer), mesosphere, thermosphere.
More solar energy reaches the equator than the poles; warm air rises at the equator and sinks near 30 degrees, creating Hadley cells and deserts there.
The Coriolis effect deflects winds right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern; trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies result.
A rain shadow forms on the leeward side of a mountain as air loses moisture while rising.

concepts.intro: Ocean circulation and Earth's tilt move heat around the planet.
b: Seasons result from the 23.5 degree axial tilt, not distance from the Sun.
Surface currents are driven by winds; thermohaline circulation is driven by differences in temperature and salinity (density).
El Nino brings warm surface water to the eastern Pacific, reduces upwelling and shifts weather; La Nina is the cool phase.
Upwelling brings nutrient-rich water to the surface and supports productive fisheries.

traps: Seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
Clay has tiny particles and high water-holding capacity, so it drains slowly; sand drains quickly.

units.name: Land and Water Use

concepts.intro: Food production relies on land, water, energy and chemicals, each with environmental trade-offs.
b: Monocultures are efficient but vulnerable to pests; crop rotation, cover crops and polyculture improve soil and reduce pests.
Tilling causes erosion; no-till, contour plowing and terracing reduce soil loss.
Irrigation: flood irrigation wastes water and can cause salinization; drip irrigation is more efficient.
Fertilizer runoff causes eutrophication; integrated pest management (IPM) combines biological, cultural and limited chemical controls.
Concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) produce large volumes of waste and use antibiotics; overgrazing can lead to desertification.

concepts.intro: Harvesting natural resources can exceed sustainable yield.
b: Overfishing, bycatch and bottom trawling harm marine populations; aquaculture can ease pressure but pollutes and spreads disease.
Clear-cutting is cheap but causes erosion and habitat loss; selective cutting and certified forestry are more sustainable.
Surface mining includes strip and mountaintop removal; acid mine drainage lowers stream pH and mobilizes metals.
Sustainable yield is the harvest that does not reduce the resource's ability to renew.

concepts.intro: Cities concentrate people and change land and water systems.
b: Urban sprawl increases car use and consumes farmland; impervious surfaces raise runoff and flooding.
The urban heat island effect makes cities warmer than surrounding areas.
Dams provide water and power but alter flow, trap sediment and displace people.
Groundwater overdraft, as with the Ogallala Aquifer, drops water tables and causes land subsidence.
Tragedy of the commons: shared resources are overused when individuals act in their own interest.

traps: Salinization comes from irrigation water evaporating and leaving salts behind.
Bycatch is the unintended catch of non-target species, not a type of aquaculture.

units.name: Energy Resources and Consumption

concepts.intro: Fossil fuels supply most energy but cause pollution and carbon emissions.
b: Coal rank by carbon content: peat, lignite, bituminous, anthracite; coal releases the most CO2 and sulfur and mercury pollutants per unit of energy.
Oil and natural gas are formed from buried marine organisms; natural gas burns cleaner than coal and oil but methane leaks are a potent greenhouse gas.
Fracking injects fluid to release oil and gas but can contaminate groundwater and trigger small earthquakes.
Fossil fuels are nonrenewable on human timescales.

concepts.intro: Low-carbon sources each have advantages and limits.
b: Nuclear fission splits uranium-235; it produces no CO2 during operation but creates long-lived radioactive waste and risk of accidents (Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, Fukushima).
Solar photovoltaics convert light to electricity; wind turbines convert wind's kinetic energy; both are intermittent and need storage or backup.
Hydroelectric power is reliable but affects rivers and fish; geothermal taps Earth's heat in suitable locations.
Biomass and biofuels can be carbon neutral if replanted but compete with food and land; hydrogen fuel cells emit only water if the hydrogen is produced cleanly.

concepts.intro: Efficiency and conservation reduce demand.
b: Energy conversions lose usable energy as heat; a power plant converts heat to electricity at about 35 to 40 percent efficiency.
Cogeneration uses waste heat from electricity production for heating, raising overall efficiency.
Conservation: insulation, efficient appliances, public transportation, smart grids and green building standards (LEED).
Units: a kilowatt-hour is the energy of one kilowatt used for one hour.

traps: Nuclear power plants do not emit CO2 when operating, but the full life cycle and waste storage still have impacts.
Natural gas is cleaner than coal in CO2 per energy but leaked methane is a much stronger greenhouse gas than CO2.

units.name: Atmospheric Pollution

concepts.intro: Air pollutants harm health and ecosystems and are regulated under the Clean Air Act.
b: Primary pollutants are emitted directly (CO, SO2, NOx, particulates, lead); secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere (ground-level ozone, sulfuric and nitric acids).
Criteria pollutants regulated by the EPA: carbon monoxide, lead, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, particulate matter and sulfur dioxide.
Catalytic converters reduce CO, NOx and hydrocarbons from cars; scrubbers remove SO2 from power plant exhaust.
Particulate matter (PM2.5) penetrates deep into lungs and is linked to heart and lung disease.

concepts.intro: Weather and chemistry combine to create pollution events.
b: Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight to produce ground-level ozone.
Industrial (gray) smog comes from burning coal and releases sulfur dioxide and particulates.
A temperature inversion traps cooler air under a layer of warm air and holds pollution near the ground.
Acid deposition forms from SO2 and NOx converting to sulfuric and nitric acid; it acidifies lakes, damages forests and corrodes buildings.

concepts.l: Indoor air and the ozone layer
concepts.intro: Pollution occurs inside buildings and high in the atmosphere.
b: Indoor pollutants include radon (a radioactive gas from soil), asbestos, carbon monoxide, mold and volatile organic compounds.
Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation; CFCs release chlorine that destroys ozone.
The Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs and is a model for international environmental agreements.
Ground-level ozone is harmful pollution, while stratospheric ozone is protective.

traps: Ozone is 'good up high, bad nearby': stratospheric ozone protects us, ground-level ozone is a pollutant.
Acid deposition includes dry deposition as well as acid rain.

units.name: Aquatic and Terrestrial Pollution

concepts.intro: Pollutants enter water from point and nonpoint sources.
b: Point sources have a single identifiable discharge (a pipe); nonpoint sources are diffuse (fertilizer and urban runoff).
Eutrophication: excess nitrogen and phosphorus cause algal blooms; decomposition of dead algae lowers dissolved oxygen and can create dead zones.
Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) measures the oxygen microorganisms need to break down organic waste.
Thermal pollution from power plants lowers oxygen solubility and stresses aquatic life.
Bioaccumulation builds up a toxin in an organism over time; biomagnification increases its concentration up the food chain (mercury, DDT).

concepts.intro: Waste management reduces harm and recovers resources.
b: Landfills produce leachate and methane; modern landfills have liners, leachate collection and gas capture.
Incineration reduces volume and can generate energy but emits pollutants and leaves toxic ash.
Reduce, reuse, recycle, and composting keep material out of landfills; reducing is the most effective step.
Superfund (CERCLA) funds cleanup of contaminated sites; RCRA regulates hazardous waste from creation to disposal.
Plastics persist for centuries and break into microplastics that enter food webs.

concepts.intro: Treatment and regulation protect water and public health.
b: Wastewater treatment: primary (physical removal of solids), secondary (biological breakdown), tertiary (chemical removal of nutrients, disinfection).
The Clean Water Act regulates discharges into surface waters; the Safe Drinking Water Act sets standards for drinking water.
Dose-response curves and LD50 describe toxicity; infectious diseases such as cholera spread through contaminated water.

traps: Biomagnification is concentration increasing up trophic levels; bioaccumulation is buildup within one organism.
The dead zone is caused by oxygen depletion after algae die and decompose, not by the algae directly using oxygen to bloom.

units.name: Global Change

concepts.intro: Greenhouse gases trap heat, and human emissions have increased their concentrations.
b: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm; the enhanced greenhouse effect results from added CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs.
Global warming potential compares gases: methane and nitrous oxide trap more heat per molecule than CO2 but are less abundant.
Feedback loops: melting ice lowers albedo and amplifies warming (positive); increased cloud cover or plant growth can dampen it (negative).
Evidence includes rising temperatures, ice-core records, shrinking glaciers and sea-level rise.

concepts.intro: Warming and related changes affect ecosystems and people.
b: Sea-level rise from thermal expansion and melting land ice threatens coastal communities and aquifers.
Ocean acidification: CO2 dissolves to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and harming corals and shellfish.
Species ranges shift, coral bleaching increases, and extreme weather events become more frequent.
Invasive species and habitat loss add to biodiversity decline.

concepts.intro: Mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation prepares for change.
b: Mitigation: renewable energy, efficiency, carbon taxes, cap-and-trade, reforestation and carbon capture.
Adaptation: sea walls, drought-resistant crops, relocating communities.
International agreements include the Montreal Protocol, the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
Individual choices (transportation, diet, energy use) and policy both matter.

traps: Weather is short-term; climate is the long-term average (about 30 years).
The ozone hole and global warming are different problems with different causes (CFCs versus CO2 and other greenhouse gases).

quiz.q: About what percentage of energy is typically transferred from one trophic level to the next?
quiz.e: Most energy is lost as heat through respiration, which is why food chains are short.

quiz.q: Net primary productivity (NPP) is calculated as:
o: GPP divided by the producers' biomass
Total solar energy minus reflected light
quiz.e: NPP is the energy available to consumers after producers use some for their own respiration.

quiz.q: Which process converts atmospheric nitrogen (N2) into ammonia that plants can use?
quiz.e: Bacteria such as Rhizobium in legume roots perform nitrogen fixation.

quiz.q: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere by converting:
quiz.e: Anaerobic bacteria carry out this step in waterlogged soil.

quiz.q: The phosphorus cycle differs from the carbon and nitrogen cycles in that it:
o: Is driven mainly by bacterial fixation
Releases most of its phosphorus as gas
Relies on denitrifying bacteria in soil
quiz.e: Phosphorus moves mainly through rock weathering, soil, water and organisms.

quiz.q: Which nutrient most often limits plant growth in freshwater lakes?
quiz.e: Added phosphorus commonly triggers algal blooms in lakes.

quiz.q: Tropical rainforest soils are typically nutrient poor because:
o: Heavy rainfall is absent so minerals rarely dissolve into soil
Most nutrients are held in the living biomass and quickly recycled
Clay particles bind all nutrients so plants cannot absorb them
Cool temperatures slow growth so little organic matter forms
quiz.e: Warm, wet conditions decompose material quickly and plants absorb nutrients before they accumulate in soil.

quiz.q: Which biome is characterized by permafrost and a short growing season?
quiz.e: Permanently frozen ground prevents deep roots and trees.

quiz.q: An estuary is an area where:
o: Fresh water and salt water mix
quiz.e: Estuaries are highly productive nurseries for many species.

quiz.q: Photosynthesis and aerobic respiration are:
o: Reverse processes where photosynthesis releases the energy stored in glucose
Roughly opposite processes that link energy flow and the carbon cycle
Both reactions that consume carbon dioxide and release oxygen to the air
Separate processes in different organisms that do not exchange carbon
quiz.e: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose; respiration releases it.

quiz.q: Which organisms are autotrophs?
o: Producers such as plants and algae
quiz.e: Autotrophs make their own food from light or chemical energy.

quiz.q: Decomposers are important because they:
o: Capture sunlight and convert it into chemical energy in glucose
Occupy the top trophic level and control predator numbers
Release oxygen into the atmosphere through photosynthesis
Recycle nutrients from dead organisms back into the ecosystem
quiz.e: Without decomposition nutrients would remain locked in dead matter.

quiz.q: A food web differs from a food chain because a food web:
o: Tracks one energy path from producer to consumer
Shows feeding within a single trophic level
Shows nutrient cycles between organisms and soil
quiz.e: Real ecosystems have many overlapping feeding links.

quiz.q: Where do coral reefs mostly occur?
o: Cold, deep polar seas with little sunlight
Dark ocean trenches with high pressure
Freshwater lakes with low salinity and cool temperatures
quiz.e: Reef-building corals rely on symbiotic algae that need sunlight and warmth.

quiz.q: In a lake, the littoral zone is the:
o: Deep, dark bottom area where no light reaches
Open water far from shore where plankton float
Layer of dead organisms decomposing on the lake floor
Shallow area near shore where light reaches the bottom
quiz.e: Rooted plants grow in the littoral zone.

quiz.q: Fall and spring lake turnover:
o: Mixes oxygen and nutrients throughout the water column
Freezes the surface water and seals the lake from the air
Removes nutrients from the lake and flushes them downstream
Halts photosynthesis by blocking light for the whole season
quiz.e: Temperature changes make surface and bottom water equal in density so they mix.

quiz.q: Wetlands provide the ecosystem service of:
o: Raising the water table above ground permanently
quiz.e: They absorb floodwater and trap pollutants and sediment.

quiz.q: Which statement about island biogeography is correct?
o: Small islands far from the mainland support the most species
Island size does not affect species number
Large islands close to the mainland support the most species
Distance from the mainland increases species number
quiz.e: Larger islands have more habitats, and nearby islands receive more colonists.

quiz.q: A keystone species is one that:
o: Supplies the largest share of the energy that flows through its ecosystem
Has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance
Is the first species to colonize an area after a disturbance has occurred
Is a species found nowhere else on Earth, with a very small natural range
quiz.e: Removing a keystone species can change the entire community, as with sea otters and kelp forests.

quiz.q: In the HIPPCO acronym for threats to biodiversity, the letter O stands for:
quiz.e: HIPPCO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, Population growth, Climate change, Overexploitation.

quiz.q: Habitat fragmentation harms populations mainly by:
o: Isolating small populations and reducing gene flow
Enlarging habitat patches and increasing gene flow
Raising local biodiversity by adding many new edge species
Eliminating habitat edges and exposing interior species
quiz.e: Smaller, isolated populations are more vulnerable to inbreeding and local extinction.

quiz.q: Wildlife corridors are designed to:
o: Keep animals out of protected areas and reduce human conflict
Connect fragmented habitat so animals can move between patches
Increase the amount of edge habitat for generalist species
Attract invasive species to stable and well-protected habitat
quiz.e: Corridors allow gene flow and migration.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a provisioning ecosystem service?
quiz.e: Provisioning services supply goods that people use directly.

quiz.q: Which is a regulating ecosystem service?
quiz.e: Regulating services moderate processes like pollination, floods and climate.

quiz.q: Primary succession begins:
o: After a forest fire in an area where soil remains intact
On bare rock or newly formed land without soil
In an abandoned farm field with existing soil and seeds
In a mature forest after a single tree falls and opens the canopy
quiz.e: Pioneer species such as lichens start building soil.

quiz.q: Secondary succession is typically faster than primary succession because:
o: There is no competition among plants after the disturbance
The climate is warmer and wetter than in primary succession
Pioneer species are not needed since the area is already forested
Soil and some seeds remain after the disturbance
quiz.e: Existing soil allows plants to colonize quickly.

quiz.q: Which characteristic usually describes a pioneer species?
o: Slow growing and tolerant of deep shade
Fast growing and tolerant of harsh conditions
Dependent on rich, deep soil for establishment
Long lived, large and common in mature forests
quiz.e: Pioneers are often r-selected and able to colonize disturbed areas.

quiz.q: Genetic diversity is important because it:
o: Reduces the number of species and simplifies food webs
Helps populations adapt to environmental change and disease
Prevents mutations and keeps traits identical across a population
Increases inbreeding and strengthens the dominant traits
quiz.e: A variety of genes increases the chance that some individuals survive a new stress.

quiz.q: An invasive species often succeeds because it:
o: Has a diet that is highly specialized to the new region
Is more susceptible to disease than the native species
Lacks natural predators or competitors in the new area
Evolved alongside the native species in the same ecosystem
quiz.e: Release from natural enemies lets its population grow.

quiz.q: Which law protects species at risk of extinction in the United States?
quiz.e: The ESA lists threatened and endangered species and protects their habitat.

quiz.q: CITES regulates:
o: Ocean fishing quotas and whaling catch limits
Greenhouse gas emissions from industrial sources
quiz.e: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species limits trade that threatens survival.

quiz.q: Species evenness refers to:
o: How similar the abundances of different species are
The total number of different species in a community
The size of the habitat that species occupy
The age and stability of the ecosystem over time
quiz.e: A community dominated by one species has low evenness.

quiz.q: A specialist species is more vulnerable to environmental change than a generalist because it:
o: Has a narrow range of habitat or food requirements
Reproduces faster and so recovers quickly after disturbance
Lives in many different habitats across wide ranges
Eats many types of food depending on availability
quiz.e: If its specific resource disappears it has few alternatives.

quiz.q: An indicator species is useful because it:
o: Protects other species automatically by its presence alone
Is the top predator that controls the populations below it
Shows the health of an ecosystem through its presence or condition
Controls the numbers of its prey and shapes the community
quiz.e: Examples include amphibians, whose sensitive skin reflects water quality.

quiz.q: A population growing exponentially produces what shape of curve?
quiz.e: Growth accelerates when resources are unlimited.

quiz.q: Logistic growth levels off at the:
quiz.e: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum population the environment can sustain.

quiz.q: Which is a density-dependent limiting factor?
o: Disease spreading faster in crowded populations
A wildfire sweeping through a forest
A volcanic eruption burying nearby populations
quiz.e: The effect of density-dependent factors increases with population density.

quiz.q: Which describes an r-selected species?
o: Many offspring and little parental care
Few offspring with extensive parental care
Long lifespan and late reproductive maturity
Large body size and stable population near carrying capacity
quiz.e: Examples include insects, weeds and many fish.

quiz.q: Which describes a K-selected species?
o: Few offspring, long life and high parental care
Rapid maturity and short life span
No parental care and high juvenile mortality
quiz.e: Elephants and humans are K-selected and more vulnerable to extinction.

quiz.q: A Type III survivorship curve shows that:
o: Most individuals live to old age
quiz.e: Species with many offspring and low early survival follow this pattern.

quiz.q: A country's population grows 2 percent per year. Using the rule of 70, its doubling time is about:
quiz.e: 70 divided by 2 equals 35.

quiz.q: A population growing 1.4 percent per year will double in about:
quiz.e: 70 divided by 1.4 equals 50.

quiz.q: Replacement-level fertility in developed countries is about:
quiz.e: It is slightly above 2 because some children do not survive to reproduce.

quiz.q: An age-structure diagram with a very wide base indicates:
quiz.e: Many young people will enter their reproductive years.

quiz.q: In the demographic transition model, rapid growth occurs when:
o: Both death rates and birth rates are high
Both death rates and birth rates are low
Birth rates fall below death rates
Death rates fall while birth rates remain high
quiz.e: Better health and food supply cut mortality first.

quiz.q: Which factor is most associated with lower fertility rates?
o: Higher infant mortality and need for more children
Lack of access to family planning and contraception
Greater education and opportunities for women
Agricultural labor needs that favor larger families
quiz.e: Education and access to contraception lead to smaller families.

quiz.q: The IPAT equation states that environmental impact equals:
quiz.e: Per-capita consumption and technology matter as much as population size.

quiz.q: A population's birth rate is 20 per 1000 and the death rate is 10 per 1000 with no migration. The growth rate is:
quiz.e: 20 minus 10 gives 10 per 1000, which is 1 percent.

quiz.q: The ecological footprint measures:
o: The number of species supported by an area of land and water
The total land area of a country and its coastline
The amount of energy transferred between levels of a food chain
The land and water needed to support a person's resource use and absorb waste
quiz.e: It lets us compare consumption with Earth's biological capacity.

quiz.q: A Type I survivorship curve is typical of:
o: Oysters and other species with huge numbers of young
Humans and other species with high parental care
Insects and other species with little parental care
Weeds and other species with many tiny seeds
quiz.e: Most individuals survive until old age.

quiz.q: Which soil horizon is called topsoil?
quiz.e: The A horizon is rich in organic matter mixed with minerals.

quiz.q: Which soil horizon is the parent material?
quiz.e: It consists of partially weathered rock.

quiz.q: Soil with a high proportion of clay will:
quiz.e: Clay particles are tiny and hold water and nutrients tightly.

quiz.q: Sandy soil is characterized by:
o: Low permeability and high water-holding capacity
High nutrient retention and strong binding of minerals
High permeability and low water-holding capacity
High organic matter and slow drainage of water
quiz.e: Large particles leave big spaces through which water drains.

quiz.q: Which atmospheric layer contains the ozone layer?
quiz.e: The stratosphere is above the troposphere and absorbs UV radiation.

quiz.q: Most weather occurs in the:
quiz.e: The troposphere contains most of the atmosphere's mass and water vapor.

quiz.q: Deserts are commonly found near 30 degrees latitude because:
o: The Sun is directly overhead there all year
Winds blow from the east and carry no moisture
Dry air sinks there after rising at the equator
Warm ocean currents evaporate water and dry the land
quiz.e: Descending air warms and holds moisture rather than releasing it.

quiz.q: The Coriolis effect causes winds in the Northern Hemisphere to be deflected:
quiz.e: Earth's rotation deflects moving air masses.

quiz.q: Seasons occur because of:
o: Earth's changing distance from the Sun
quiz.e: Tilt changes the angle and length of sunlight in each hemisphere.

quiz.q: A rain shadow forms on the:
o: Windward side of a mountain range
Coastal side of a mountain range
Leeward side of a mountain range
quiz.e: Air loses moisture as it rises, so the far side is dry.

quiz.q: During an El Nino event, the eastern Pacific typically experiences:
o: Colder surface water and enhanced upwelling
Warmer surface water and reduced upwelling
Stronger trade winds and abundant nutrient supply
quiz.e: Fisheries decline because nutrient-rich water no longer reaches the surface.

quiz.q: Upwelling is beneficial to fisheries because it:
o: Brings nutrient-rich deep water to the surface
Cools the air and reduces coastal temperatures
Reduces salinity by mixing in freshwater
Blocks sunlight and slows algal growth
quiz.e: Nutrients support plankton, the base of the food web.

quiz.q: Thermohaline circulation is driven by differences in:
quiz.e: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks.

quiz.q: A divergent plate boundary typically produces:
o: Deep trenches where one plate is pulled under another
Large mountain ranges formed by colliding plates
New crust at a mid-ocean ridge or rift
Transform faults where plates slide sideways past each other
quiz.e: Plates move apart and magma rises to fill the gap.

quiz.q: Volcanic eruptions can temporarily cool climate because they:
o: Release large amounts of CO2 that trap heat
Increase solar output reaching the upper atmosphere
Inject aerosols into the stratosphere that reflect sunlight
Raise sea level by melting glaciers near the volcano
quiz.e: Sulfate aerosols increase albedo.

quiz.q: Which soil component holds the most nutrients and water, improving fertility?
quiz.e: Humus improves structure and holds nutrients.

quiz.q: Which practice reduces soil erosion on slopes?
quiz.e: These practices slow water runoff.

quiz.q: No-till farming helps by:
o: Increasing tilling to loosen soil and bury weeds
Leaving soil undisturbed to reduce erosion and retain moisture
Removing crop residue so the field warms faster
Using more fertilizer to replace lost nutrients
quiz.e: Roots and residue hold soil in place.

quiz.q: Over time, irrigation can cause salinization because:
o: Salts dissolve in rain and wash into the soil
Plant roots release salt into the surrounding soil
Soil minerals produce salt as they decompose
Water evaporates and leaves salts behind in the soil
quiz.e: Salt buildup reduces crop yields.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method is most water efficient?
o: Spray irrigation in hot, windy weather
quiz.e: Water is delivered directly to plant roots with little evaporation.

quiz.q: Integrated pest management (IPM) is best described as:
o: Relying on pesticide sprays whenever any pests are seen, plus some crop rotation
Using a combination of biological, cultural and limited chemical controls
Releasing a non-native predator into a field to remove a pest species
Growing pest-resistant genetically modified crops, with pesticide as the main tool
quiz.e: IPM minimizes chemical use while controlling pests.

quiz.q: A main environmental concern of monoculture farming is:
quiz.e: Genetically uniform crops can be wiped out by a single pest.

quiz.q: Bycatch refers to:
o: Fish raised in farms and sold to markets
Fish caught for sport and released unharmed
Unintended capture of non-target species during fishing
Fishing that breaks laws or exceeds legal quotas
quiz.e: Bottom trawling and drift nets create large amounts of bycatch.

quiz.q: Overfishing leads to:
o: Fish stocks that increase as catch rates rise
Populations declining faster than they can replace themselves
Greater genetic diversity within harvested populations
Reduced fishing pressure as fleets move elsewhere
quiz.e: Harvests that exceed sustainable yield cause stock collapse.

quiz.q: Clear-cutting a forest most directly causes:
o: Increased soil nutrients from rapidly decomposing logs
Reduced runoff because bare soil absorbs more water
Increased soil erosion and habitat loss
Greater biodiversity as more sunlight reaches the ground
quiz.e: Removing all trees exposes soil.

quiz.q: Acid mine drainage results when:
o: Mines are filled with soil and covered with vegetation
Coal is burned and sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain
Fertilizer runs off fields and washes into streams
Water reacts with exposed sulfide minerals, forming sulfuric acid
quiz.e: It lowers stream pH and dissolves toxic metals.

quiz.q: Impervious surfaces in cities increase:
quiz.e: Pavement prevents infiltration.

quiz.q: The urban heat island effect occurs because cities:
o: Absorb and retain heat from dark surfaces and have fewer plants
Have higher albedo surfaces that reflect heat back toward space
Receive more solar radiation than rural areas because of their latitude
Lose heat quickly at night because of tall buildings and open space
quiz.e: Concrete and asphalt store heat.

quiz.q: The Ogallala Aquifer is being depleted mainly because:
o: It is polluted by oil leaks from surface wells
It is too deep to be reached by modern pumps
It is a surface lake that is drying from evaporation
Water is withdrawn for irrigation faster than it recharges
quiz.e: Overdraft lowers the water table.

quiz.q: Groundwater overdraft in coastal areas can lead to:
quiz.e: Lowering freshwater pressure lets seawater move inland.

quiz.q: The tragedy of the commons describes:
o: Overuse of a shared resource when individuals act in their own interest
Underuse of a shared resource when individuals choose to cooperate with others
Collapse of a shared resource when governments restrict how much anyone may use
Unequal sharing of resources when wealthy people control most of the supply
quiz.e: Each user gains from using more while the cost is shared.

quiz.q: A major environmental concern of concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) is:
o: Reduced antibiotic use compared to open pasture
Lower water use compared to grazing systems
Large amounts of concentrated animal waste
quiz.e: Waste can contaminate water and air.

quiz.q: Which type of coal has the highest carbon content and energy content?
quiz.e: Rank increases from peat to lignite to bituminous to anthracite.

quiz.q: Burning coal is a major source of:
o: Sulfur dioxide, mercury and carbon dioxide
quiz.e: Coal contains sulfur and trace metals in addition to carbon.

quiz.q: Which fossil fuel produces the least CO2 per unit of energy when burned?
quiz.e: Methane has a high hydrogen-to-carbon ratio.

quiz.q: A major climate concern with natural gas is:
o: Its high sulfur content that causes acid rain
Heavy metal emissions such as mercury and lead
Leaks of methane, a potent greenhouse gas
It produces no CO2 when burned, so offsets are needed
quiz.e: Methane traps more heat per molecule than CO2.

quiz.q: Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) involves:
o: Mining coal from the surface by removing mountaintops
Drilling deep wells to tap geothermal heat for power
Burning natural gas to generate electricity at plants
Injecting high-pressure fluid to fracture rock and release oil or gas
quiz.e: Concerns include groundwater contamination and induced earthquakes.

quiz.q: Nuclear fission generates energy by:
quiz.e: Splitting heavy nuclei releases heat to make steam.

quiz.q: A major drawback of nuclear power is:
quiz.e: Spent fuel remains radioactive for thousands of years.

quiz.q: Which nuclear accident occurred in Ukraine in 1986?
quiz.e: A reactor explosion released large amounts of radiation.

quiz.q: Solar photovoltaic cells convert:
quiz.e: Photons knock electrons loose in semiconductor material.

quiz.q: A main limitation of solar and wind power is:
o: Intermittency, which requires storage or backup power
High air pollution from burning fuel during operation
Large CO2 emissions released during operation
Scarcity of fuel supplies as resources are depleted
quiz.e: Output varies with weather and time of day.

quiz.q: A downside of large hydroelectric dams is that they:
o: Emit large amounts of CO2 while generating power
Alter river flow, trap sediment and affect fish migration
Require fuel deliveries that raise operating costs
Cause acid rain by releasing sulfur dioxide
quiz.e: They also flood land and displace communities.

quiz.q: Geothermal energy comes from:
quiz.e: It is best where hot rock lies near the surface.

quiz.q: Biofuels such as ethanol can be considered carbon neutral when:
o: The fuel is made from crops grown using fossil-fuel fertilizers
The crop is grown on land that was cleared from mature forest
The CO2 released is lower than gasoline but is not offset by regrowth
The CO2 released equals the CO2 absorbed by regrowing the crop
quiz.e: Their carbon was recently taken from the atmosphere.

quiz.q: A hydrogen fuel cell produces:
quiz.e: Hydrogen combines with oxygen without combustion.

quiz.q: A coal power plant that is 35 percent efficient converts what portion of the fuel energy into electricity?
quiz.e: The rest is lost as waste heat.

quiz.q: Cogeneration improves efficiency by:
o: Burning more fuel to produce extra electricity
Using less insulation to let heat escape the plant
Capturing waste heat for another use
Generating electricity from wind to reduce fuel use
quiz.e: Waste heat can supply heating, so more of the energy is used.

quiz.q: Which is an example of energy conservation?
quiz.e: Reducing demand lowers emissions and cost.

quiz.q: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of:
quiz.e: One kilowatt used for one hour.

quiz.q: A 100-watt bulb runs for 10 hours. How much energy does it use?
Which is a secondary air pollutant?
quiz.e: Secondary pollutants form from reactions among primary pollutants.

quiz.q: Photochemical smog forms when:
o: SO2 and water react in clouds
NOx and VOCs react in sunlight
Coal soot and SO2 mix with fog
quiz.e: The key product is ground-level ozone.

quiz.q: Industrial smog is mainly associated with:
o: Car exhaust reacting with sunlight, producing ozone
Burning coal, producing sulfur dioxide and particulates
Ozone depletion in the stratosphere over cities
Methane released from landfills and livestock
quiz.e: It is also called gray-air smog.

quiz.q: A temperature inversion makes air pollution worse because it:
o: Cools the upper atmosphere and lifts pollutants away
Traps cool air and pollutants under a layer of warm air
Increases wind speed and spreads pollutants widely
Removes pollutants by washing them out of the air
quiz.e: There is little vertical mixing.

quiz.q: Acid deposition is caused mainly by emissions of:
quiz.e: They form sulfuric and nitric acids in the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Acid rain harms lakes by:
o: Lowering pH and releasing toxic aluminum from soil
Raising pH and making the water more basic
Adding nutrients that trigger algal blooms
Raising water temperature and lowering oxygen
quiz.e: Many aquatic species cannot survive low pH.

quiz.q: A catalytic converter in a car reduces emissions of:
o: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor
Carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons
quiz.e: It converts them to less harmful gases.

quiz.q: Scrubbers on power plants remove:
quiz.e: They react the gas with a sorbent like limestone.

quiz.q: The Clean Air Act regulates:
o: Water quality in rivers, lakes and drinking supplies
Criteria air pollutants such as ozone and particulates
Hazardous waste disposal from creation to cleanup
Endangered species and the habitats they depend on
quiz.e: The EPA sets national standards.

quiz.q: Radon is a health concern because it is a:
o: Heavy metal that builds up in fish and shellfish
Greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere
Radioactive gas that can accumulate indoors and cause lung cancer
Pesticide that persists in soil and enters groundwater
quiz.e: It seeps from soil and rock into basements.

quiz.q: Which indoor pollutant is released by some building materials and paints?
quiz.e: VOCs off-gas from many products.

quiz.q: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage the ozone layer by:
o: Absorbing sunlight and warming the stratosphere
Adding carbon dioxide that traps heat in the lower atmosphere
Releasing chlorine atoms that break down ozone
Cooling the stratosphere until ozone molecules freeze
quiz.e: One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.

quiz.q: The Montreal Protocol is notable because it:
o: Limited carbon emissions across many countries
Banned all plastics and reduced marine pollution
Protected endangered species and their habitats
quiz.e: It is often cited as a successful international agreement.

quiz.q: Ozone in the stratosphere is beneficial because it:
o: Causes smog and irritates human lungs
Warms the troposphere by trapping infrared heat
Produces oxygen that animals need to breathe
quiz.e: Ground-level ozone, by contrast, is harmful.

quiz.q: Which particulate size is most dangerous to human health?
o: PM100, because it is the largest and most abundant
Large dust, because it scratches the lungs
PM2.5, because it penetrates deep into the lungs
Pollen, because it triggers allergies in all people
quiz.e: Fine particles can enter the bloodstream.

quiz.q: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it:
o: Burns the skin on contact with exposed tissue
Causes acid rain by dissolving in cloud water
Destroys ozone high in the stratosphere
Binds to hemoglobin, reducing oxygen delivery
quiz.e: It is produced by incomplete combustion.

quiz.q: A point source of water pollution is:
o: A discharge pipe from a factory
quiz.e: Point sources are single, identifiable locations.

quiz.q: Which is a nonpoint source of pollution?
quiz.e: Nonpoint sources are diffuse and harder to regulate.

quiz.q: Eutrophication is caused by:
o: Too little oxygen added to the water by humans
Excess nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, in water
Cold temperatures that slow decomposition in lakes
Excess salt washing in from roads and irrigation
quiz.e: Nutrients trigger algal blooms.

quiz.q: After an algal bloom dies, dissolved oxygen drops because:
o: Dead algae release toxins that bind dissolved oxygen
Fish use up the oxygen that the algae had produced
Decomposers use oxygen to break down dead algae
Dead algae form a layer that blocks oxygen from air
quiz.e: Aerobic decomposition consumes oxygen.

quiz.q: A high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) indicates:
o: Clean water with few organisms and little waste
High dissolved oxygen and healthy fish populations
Large amounts of organic waste in the water
Low temperature and slow microbial activity
quiz.e: Microorganisms need oxygen to decompose the waste.

quiz.q: Thermal pollution harms aquatic life because warm water:
quiz.e: Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises.

quiz.q: Biomagnification is the:
o: Buildup of a toxin within the body of one organism
Increase in toxin concentration at higher trophic levels
Breakdown of toxins by bacteria in the environment
Dilution of toxins as they spread through water
quiz.e: Top predators carry the highest concentrations.

quiz.q: Which substance is a classic example of biomagnification?
quiz.e: Fat-soluble or persistent toxins concentrate up the food chain.

quiz.q: A modern landfill reduces groundwater contamination mainly by using:
o: Open burning of waste to reduce volume
Leaving waste without any cover or lining
Digging larger holes so waste is buried deeper
quiz.e: Leachate is liquid that has passed through waste.

quiz.q: Landfills produce which greenhouse gas as waste decomposes without oxygen?
quiz.e: Many landfills capture it for energy.

quiz.q: Which is the most effective waste management strategy?
quiz.e: Reducing consumption prevents waste altogether.

quiz.q: Superfund (CERCLA) is used to:
o: Regulate drinking water quality for public systems
Clean up contaminated hazardous waste sites
Protect endangered species and their habitats
Limit air pollution from factories and vehicles
quiz.e: It charges responsible parties for cleanup.

quiz.q: RCRA regulates:
o: Air quality standards for common pollutants
Ocean dumping of waste from ships
Hazardous waste from creation to disposal
quiz.e: It is known as the 'cradle-to-grave' law.

quiz.q: Secondary wastewater treatment uses:
o: Screens that remove large objects from incoming water
Chlorine alone to disinfect the water
Sand filters alone to trap small particles
Microorganisms to break down organic matter
quiz.e: Primary treatment removes solids physically.

quiz.q: The LD50 of a substance is the dose that:
o: Kills 50 percent of a test population
Kills 10 percent of a test population
Affects 50 percent of a test population
Kills 90 percent of a test population
quiz.e: A lower LD50 indicates higher toxicity.

quiz.q: Microplastics are a concern because they:
o: Break down quickly into harmless compounds
Increase soil fertility by adding nutrients
Add oxygen to water as they degrade
Persist in the environment and enter food webs
quiz.e: Plastics can last for centuries.

quiz.q: The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is largely caused by:
o: Oil spills from offshore drilling platforms
Overfishing of shrimp and other commercial species
Nutrient runoff from the Mississippi River basin
Warm currents that carry away dissolved oxygen
quiz.e: Fertilizer from farmland feeds algal blooms.

quiz.q: Cholera spreads mainly through:
quiz.e: Poor sanitation is a major risk factor.

quiz.q: Which gas contributes most to the enhanced greenhouse effect because of its large quantity?
quiz.e: CO2 is emitted in enormous quantities from fossil fuels.

quiz.q: Methane has a higher global warming potential than carbon dioxide because it:
quiz.e: But it is present in much smaller quantities and has a shorter lifetime.

quiz.q: The melting of Arctic sea ice is an example of a positive feedback because:
o: Less ice raises albedo, reflecting more heat and causing further cooling
Less ice lowers albedo, absorbing more heat and causing more melting
More ice forms in winter, trapping heat beneath it and causing more melting
Melting ice releases cold water, which cools the ocean and slows more melting
quiz.e: Positive feedback amplifies the original change.

quiz.q: Albedo is the:
o: Amount of heat absorbed by a surface from sunlight
Temperature of the atmosphere near the surface
Fraction of sunlight reflected by a surface
Concentration of CO2 in the air above a surface
quiz.e: Snow and ice have high albedo.

quiz.q: Sea-level rise is caused by:
o: Melting of floating sea ice and ocean evaporation
Thermal expansion of seawater and melting of land ice
Increased evaporation and rainfall over the ocean
Tides and storm surges raising the water level
quiz.e: Floating ice already displaces its own weight.

quiz.q: Ocean acidification occurs when:
o: CO2 dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid
SO2 enters the ocean and forms sulfuric acid
Salt increases and changes the water chemistry
Oxygen increases and lowers the pH
quiz.e: Lower pH makes it harder for shell-building organisms to form shells.

quiz.q: Coral bleaching is caused mainly by:
o: Ocean acidification that dissolves the coral skeleton directly
Excess nutrient runoff that triggers algae to overgrow corals
Cooler water that causes corals to expel symbiotic algae
Warmer water that stresses corals and expels symbiotic algae
quiz.e: Without algae the coral loses color and food.

quiz.q: Which is a mitigation strategy for climate change?
quiz.e: Mitigation reduces emissions; the others are adaptation.

quiz.q: Which is an adaptation strategy?
o: Switching to solar power to reduce emissions
Building sea walls to protect coasts
Planting forests to absorb CO2 from the air
Using electric cars to cut emissions from transport
quiz.e: Adaptation helps communities cope with impacts.

quiz.q: A carbon tax is designed to:
o: Subsidize fossil fuels to keep energy prices low
Ban all emissions from industrial facilities
Increase emissions by lowering the cost of fuel
Put a price on carbon emissions to encourage reductions
quiz.e: It makes polluters pay for the external cost.

quiz.q: Cap-and-trade systems work by:
o: Setting a tax on each ton of emissions and letting prices adjust
Setting a limit on total emissions and allowing permits to be traded
Requiring each facility to install the best available pollution control
Subsidizing clean energy while capping the output of each factory
quiz.e: The cap is lowered over time.

quiz.q: The Kyoto Protocol:
o: Phased out ozone-depleting chemicals in developed countries
Set binding emission reduction targets for developed countries
Set binding emission targets that applied to the United States
Created a fund for developing nations to pay for climate adaptation
quiz.e: It was adopted in 1997.

quiz.q: The Paris Agreement relies on:
o: Nationally determined contributions to reduce emissions
A single global tax on all carbon emissions
A ban on all fossil fuel use by 2050
Binding fines on countries that miss targets
quiz.e: Countries set their own targets and report progress.

quiz.q: Climate differs from weather because climate is:
o: The temperature and rainfall of a single day or a single week
The short-term conditions at one place, like a storm lasting hours
The average of conditions over long periods, about 30 years
The average of conditions over one season, about three months long
quiz.e: Weather is short term.

quiz.q: Ice cores provide evidence of past climate by:
o: Preserving trapped air bubbles and isotopes that show past temperature and CO2
Counting annual layers of sediment that show how much rain fell over the centuries
Preserving fossilized pollen grains that show past plant types and nearby ocean salinity
Trapping volcanic ash layers whose thickness shows past solar output and sea level
quiz.e: They reveal hundreds of thousands of years of data.

quiz.q: Which human activity is the largest source of CO2 emissions?
quiz.e: Fossil fuel combustion is the dominant source.

quiz.q: Deforestation contributes to climate change by:
o: Adding oxygen to the air and cooling the climate
Cooling the area by exposing bare soil to wind
Removing trees that absorb CO2 and often releasing stored carbon
Increasing local rainfall and absorbing more heat
quiz.e: Burning or decomposing trees releases CO2.

quiz.q: The ozone hole is primarily caused by:
quiz.e: It is a different problem from global warming.

The total rate at which producers capture energy through photosynthesis.
GPP minus the energy producers use in respiration; the energy available to consumers.
Only about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next.
Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen (N2) into ammonia by bacteria or lightning.
Conversion of nitrate into nitrogen gas by anaerobic bacteria, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.
The nutrient in shortest supply, which restricts growth in an ecosystem.
A coastal area where fresh water from rivers mixes with salt water; highly productive.
A large region defined by its climate and characteristic plant and animal communities.
An organism, such as an earthworm, that feeds on dead organic matter.
The variety of life, including genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
Benefits that ecosystems provide to people, such as food, water filtration, pollination and recreation.
A species with a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance.
A species whose presence or condition reflects the health of an ecosystem.
A theory that larger islands closer to a mainland have more species.
The breaking of a large habitat into smaller isolated patches.
A non-native species that spreads and harms ecosystems, often without natural predators.
Ecological change that begins on bare rock or new land without soil.
Ecological change that follows a disturbance in an area where soil remains.
The first species to colonize a barren or disturbed area, such as lichens.
The maximum population size an environment can sustain over time.
Growth at a constant percentage rate that produces a J-shaped curve.
Growth that slows and levels off at carrying capacity, producing an S-shaped curve.
Species with many offspring, little parental care and rapid reproduction.
Species with few offspring, long lives and extensive parental care.
A limiting factor whose effect grows with population density, such as disease.
The average number of children a woman is expected to have in her lifetime.
Doubling time in years is about 70 divided by the percent growth rate.
The shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a society develops.
The area of land and water needed to supply a person's resources and absorb their waste.
A distinct layer of soil, such as O, A, E, B or C.
How easily water flows through soil.
The lowest layer of the atmosphere, where weather occurs.
The atmospheric layer above the troposphere that contains the ozone layer.
The deflection of moving air and water caused by Earth's rotation.
A large air circulation near the equator in which warm air rises and sinks near 30 degrees latitude.
A dry region on the leeward side of a mountain range.
A climate pattern with warm eastern Pacific surface water and reduced upwelling.
The rise of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface.
Deep ocean circulation driven by differences in water temperature and salinity.
Growing a single crop over a large area.
Planting different crops in sequence on the same land to maintain soil fertility and reduce pests.
Planting crops without plowing to reduce erosion and retain moisture.
Buildup of salts in soil, often caused by irrigation in dry regions.
A strategy combining biological, cultural and limited chemical pest controls.
Unintended catch of non-target species in fishing.
The amount of a resource that can be harvested without reducing its ability to renew.
Acidic water formed when water reacts with exposed sulfide minerals at mines.
A city that is warmer than surrounding areas because of heat-absorbing surfaces.
Overuse and depletion of a shared resource by individuals acting in their own interest.
The highest rank of coal, with the greatest carbon and energy content.
Hydraulic fracturing: injecting fluid underground to release trapped oil or natural gas.
Splitting of heavy atomic nuclei, such as uranium-235, to release energy.
A device that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
Organic material, such as wood or crop waste, used as fuel.
Energy obtained from Earth's internal heat.
A device that combines hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity and water.
Using waste heat from electricity production for another purpose, increasing efficiency.
A unit of energy equal to one kilowatt used for one hour.
A source, like solar or wind, whose output varies with weather and time.
A pollutant emitted directly from a source, such as carbon monoxide.
A pollutant formed by reactions among other pollutants in the atmosphere, such as ozone.
Air pollution formed when nitrogen oxides and VOCs react in sunlight to create ozone.
A layer of warm air over cooler air that traps pollutants near the ground.
Wet or dry deposition of sulfuric and nitric acids formed from SO2 and NOx.
A car device that converts CO, NOx and hydrocarbons into less harmful gases.
A device that removes pollutants, such as sulfur dioxide, from exhaust gases.
A radioactive gas from soil and rock that can accumulate in buildings.
Chemicals that release chlorine in the stratosphere and destroy ozone.
International agreement that phased out ozone-depleting substances.
A single, identifiable source of pollution, such as a discharge pipe.
A diffuse source of pollution, such as agricultural or urban runoff.
Nutrient enrichment that causes algal blooms and oxygen depletion in water.
An area of water with too little dissolved oxygen to support most life.
The amount of oxygen microorganisms use to decompose organic matter in water.
The buildup of a substance in an organism over time.
The increase in concentration of a toxin at higher trophic levels.
Liquid that has passed through waste and picked up contaminants.
U.S. law that funds and enforces cleanup of hazardous waste sites.
The dose of a substance that kills 50 percent of a test population.
Warming caused by gases in the atmosphere that trap outgoing heat.
A measure of how much heat a gas traps compared with carbon dioxide.
The fraction of sunlight reflected by a surface.
A process in which a change causes further change in the same direction.
Lowering of ocean pH as seawater absorbs carbon dioxide.
Loss of color when stressed corals expel their symbiotic algae.
Actions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions or remove them from the atmosphere.
Actions that help people and ecosystems cope with the effects of climate change.
A fee on carbon emissions meant to encourage reductions.
A system that limits total emissions and lets participants trade emission permits.

PART_A.q: Energy flows through an ecosystem in what pattern?
o: One direction, with energy lost as heat at each level
PART_A.e: Unlike matter, energy is not recycled; it enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

PART_A.q: Which pair of processes forms a loop that links the flow of carbon through living things?
PART_A.e: Producers take in CO2 and release O2; respiration does the reverse.

PART_A.q: Which biome has the greatest species diversity?
PART_A.e: Warm, wet and stable conditions support many species.

PART_A.q: In a lake during summer stratification, the bottom layer is most likely to have:
PART_A.e: The bottom does not mix with the oxygen-rich surface and decomposers use up oxygen.

PART_A.q: Which of the following best describes ecosystem resilience?
o: The number of species in the ecosystem
The ability of an ecosystem to recover from disturbance
PART_A.e: Diverse ecosystems often recover more quickly.

PART_A.q: A scientist removes a predator and the prey population explodes, destroying vegetation. The predator is most likely a:
PART_A.e: Its effect on the community was far larger than its abundance.

PART_A.q: The introduction of an invasive species is harmful primarily because it may:
PART_A.e: Invasives can displace natives and alter the ecosystem.

PART_A.q: A population has a growth rate of 3.5 percent. About how long until it doubles?
Which population is most likely to experience rapid growth in the future?
o: One with a large proportion of people under 15
One with a large proportion over 65
PART_A.e: Many young people will soon reproduce.

PART_A.q: Which is a density-independent factor?
PART_A.e: Its effect does not depend on population density.

PART_A.q: Which factor is most likely to lower a country's birth rate over time?
o: Increased access to education and health care for women
PART_A.e: Better opportunities lead to smaller families.

PART_A.q: Which layer of soil contains the most organic matter?
PART_A.e: The top layers contain decomposing plant material and humus.

PART_A.q: Why are many of the world's deserts found near 30 degrees north and south latitude?
o: Air descends and warms, so it holds moisture
PART_A.e: Dry, descending air suppresses rain.

PART_A.q: Which of these is caused by the tilt of Earth's axis?
PART_A.e: Tilt changes the intensity and length of sunlight during the year.

PART_A.q: Which ocean process most directly supports productive fisheries?
PART_A.e: It brings nutrients to the sunlit surface.

PART_A.q: Which agricultural practice is most likely to increase soil salinity?
o: Flood irrigation in an arid climate
PART_A.e: Evaporation concentrates salts at the surface.

PART_A.q: Which of the following would reduce the nutrient runoff from a farm field?
o: Planting a buffer strip of vegetation
Tilling up and down the slope
PART_A.e: Plants absorb nutrients and slow runoff.

PART_A.q: What is the primary environmental problem with clear-cutting?
PART_A.e: Soil is left exposed and habitats are removed.

PART_A.q: Surface mining of coal commonly leads to:
PART_A.e: Exposed minerals react with water and air.

PART_A.q: Which energy source has the lowest greenhouse gas emissions during operation?
PART_A.e: Wind turbines do not burn fuel.

PART_A.q: A power plant burns coal to produce 100 units of energy, and 60 units are lost as heat. The plant's efficiency is:
PART_A.e: 40 useful units divided by 100 is 40 percent.

PART_A.q: Which of the following is a renewable energy source?
PART_A.e: Biomass can be replenished on human timescales.

PART_A.q: Which of the following contributes most directly to the formation of ground-level ozone?
o: Nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds
PART_A.e: Sunlight drives the reaction.

PART_A.q: Acid deposition most strongly affects:

workedExamples.title: Energy transfer up a food chain
workedExamples.prompt: A grassland has 20,000 kcal of energy in producers. How much reaches secondary consumers using the 10 percent rule?
steps: Producers to primary consumers: 20,000 x 0.10 = 2,000 kcal.
Primary to secondary consumers: 2,000 x 0.10 = 200 kcal.
Secondary consumers receive 200 kcal.

workedExamples.title: Doubling time with the rule of 70
workedExamples.prompt: A population grows 2.5 percent per year. About how long until it doubles?
steps: Write the rule: doubling time = 70 / growth rate (in percent).
Substitute the rate: 70 / 2.5.
Calculate the result.

workedExamples.title: Population growth rate
workedExamples.prompt: A country has 15 births and 7 deaths per 1000 people each year and no migration. What is the annual growth rate as a percent?
steps: Net change per 1000: 15 - 7 = 8.
Convert per 1000 to a percent by dividing by 10: 8 / 10.
Report the percent.

workedExamples.title: Energy use in kilowatt-hours
workedExamples.prompt: A 1500 W space heater runs 4 hours a day for 30 days. How many kWh does it use, and what does it cost at $0.12 per kWh?
steps: Convert watts to kilowatts: 1500 W = 1.5 kW.
Energy: 1.5 kW x 4 h x 30 days = 180 kWh.

workedExamples.title: Power plant efficiency
workedExamples.prompt: A power plant burns fuel containing 500 MJ and produces 150 MJ of electricity. What is its efficiency and how much energy is lost?
steps: Efficiency = useful output / input x 100.
Energy lost as heat = 500 - 150 = 350 MJ.
workedExamples.answer: 30 percent efficiency; 350 MJ lost as heat

workedExamples.title: Biomagnification calculation
workedExamples.prompt: A toxin is 0.5 ppm in algae. Each trophic level increases concentration tenfold. What is the concentration in a fish that is a tertiary consumer (algae to zooplankton to small fish to large fish)?
steps: Count the transfers: algae to zooplankton, small fish, large fish is 3 transfers.
Each transfer multiplies by 10: 0.5 x 10 x 10 x 10.
Calculate the result.

workedExamples.title: Dissolved oxygen and temperature
workedExamples.prompt: Why does a warm discharge from a power plant lower dissolved oxygen downstream?
steps: Gas solubility decreases as water temperature increases.
Warmer water also speeds up the respiration of aquatic organisms and decomposers.
Together these lower the oxygen available to fish.
workedExamples.answer: Warmer water holds less oxygen and organisms use it faster.

workedExamples.title: Carbon emissions from driving
workedExamples.prompt: A car gets 25 miles per gallon and burning one gallon of gasoline releases about 20 pounds of CO2. How much CO2 is released driving 500 miles?
steps: Gallons used: 500 / 25 = 20 gallons.
CO2: 20 gallons x 20 lb per gallon.
Report the total.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a positive feedback loop
workedExamples.prompt: Explain how melting Arctic sea ice is a positive feedback loop.
steps: Warming melts sea ice, exposing darker ocean water.
Darker surfaces have lower albedo and absorb more sunlight.
More absorbed energy produces more warming and more melting.
workedExamples.answer: Melting lowers albedo, which causes additional warming and more melting.
